title: Series-first busbar topology cuts high-current interconnect cross-section
description: Lower per-branch current → thinner/narrower busbars → direct Al/Cu mass and cost reduction. Fewer parallel cells per node → fewer tab-to-busbar welds → less joining labour and scrap. Lower I²R also reduces cooling burden marginally. Baseline: 400V-legacy packs carried to 800V often keep large parallel groups (e.g. 2P–4P) fed by heavy busbars sized for high group current. Proposal: reconfigure the interconnect so cells are strung series-first into fewer parallel branches (e.g. 1P/2P large-format), pushing pack voltage up and per-branch current down. Physics: at 800V the same power flows at ~half the current of 400V; busbar cross-section scales with current (I²R and ampacity), so a series-heavy topology lets busbar cross-section — and thus Al/Cu mass — drop roughly with the current reduction. Fewer parallel joints per node also means fewer welds. This is the interconnect-level consequence of true 800V native design vs a re-badged 400V layout.

title: Flex-PCB main HV busbar for module-to-module interconnect
description: Replaces multiple rigid busbars + heat-shrink + many bolted lugs with fewer flex bridges; flex tolerance absorption reduces fit rejects and rework. Laminated dielectric deletes sleeving labour. Fewer torque operations. Baseline: rigid stamped Cu module-to-module HV links, hand-bolted with torqued M6/M8 lugs and insulated with heat-shrink — heavy, requires precise module-position tolerance, and each bolted joint is a resistance/inspection point. Proposal: a heavy-copper flex-PCB / laminated flexible busbar (multiple 105–210µm Cu layers on polyimide, or a laminated multi-foil Cu ribbon) forming the module-to-module HV bridges. Physics: stacking thin Cu foils achieves the required ampacity while the laminate remains flexible, absorbing module-position tolerance (±1–2mm) and thermal expansion without stress at the joint; the flex form removes the need for a rigid bar bent to exact geometry and lets one flex part span multiple modules. Integrated dielectric layer replaces heat-shrink.

title: Anodised-aluminium busbar with laser-ablated weld windows
description: One anodise process delivers insulation + corrosion protection, deleting the polymer insulation material/labour and separate corrosion coat. Laser ablation replaces masking. Durable integral layer cuts field HV-isolation warranty returns from sleeve damage. Baseline: Al busbars require a separate insulation layer (sleeve/coat) and often a plated coupon or masking step for the weld zone, plus a corrosion coat. Proposal: hard-anodise the stamped Al 1050A busbar to grow a 15–30µm Al2O3 layer that is simultaneously the dielectric insulation and the corrosion barrier, then laser-ablate only the tab-weld and terminal windows to expose bare Al for welding. Physics: anodic Al2O3 has ~10–15 kV/mm dielectric strength, so a ~25µm layer isolates 800V with margin and is far harder and more abrasion/vibration-durable than polymer sleeving; it is integral (grown from the substrate) so it cannot peel. Laser ablation cleanly reopens weld windows to bare metal in one pass, giving oxide-free weld surface

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline Western 800V packs (Taycan J1, EVA2) carry a discrete closed-loop fluxgate/Hall current transducer (LEM-class, ~€25–40) plus a separate 100µΩ shunt for redundancy, each with its own bracket and 2-wire harness. Adds a laser-weld of two sense taps (shared cell) and a Manganin-insert friction-weld on the busbar (offline sub-supply). BDU PCB gains one sigma-delta channel — no new station. Net one assembly station removed, cycle time -6s/pack.

title: Impedance-spectroscopy BMS deletes discrete SoH/temp sensors
description: Deletes a portion of the NTC array and its harness/connector poles by making cells self-sensing for temperature; the excitation hardware is a modest AFE addition or reuses balance FETs. Net sensor BOM down ~€6–10/pack while adding warranty-valuable SoH data. Baseline: SoH and cell temperature are inferred from separate NTC sensors plus coulomb counting, requiring the full NTC harness. Proposal: add a small excitation stage to the CSC AFE (or reuse the balance FETs as a switched load) to inject a mHz–kHz probe current and measure the complex cell impedance (EIS-lite). The imaginary and real impedance components map to both internal temperature (impedance is strongly temperature-dependent below ~100Hz) and state-of-health (charge-transfer resistance growth). Physics: the cell's electrochemical impedance encodes core temperature and aging directly — the cell becomes its own sensor. This deletes the need for a dedicated NTC per cell-group where impedance-derived temperature meets accuracy

ideaData.title: Software HVIL via HV plausibility deletes physical interlock loop
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the HV interlock loop (HVIL) is a continuous low-voltage series wire threaded through every HV connector and the service disconnect, with dedicated pins in every connector and a monitoring circuit — a whole parallel wiring system whose sole job is detecting an opened HV connection. Proposal: replace the physical loop with software-based HV integrity monitoring: the BMS continuously measures isolation resistance (existing IMD), HV bus continuity and pack-vs-inverter voltage plausibility; an opened HV connector is detected as a voltage/isolation discontinuity within the safety reaction time, triggering contactor open. Physics/rationale: opening any HV joint produces an immediate, measurable electrical signature (loss of continuity, isolation change) that the BMS already has the sensors to see — the dedicated HVIL wire is redundant instrumentation. This deletes 2 pins from every HV connector plus the entire interlock harness.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the HVIL harness, its dedicated pins in every HV connector (2 poles × many connectors), and its monitoring input. Reduces connector complexity and one whole wiring subsystem. Net ~€6–12/pack plus simpler, cheaper connectors and fewer assembly routes.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Deletes HVIL harness routing and the per-connector interlock-pin population; HV connectors become simpler/cheaper SKUs. Deletes HVIL continuity EOL test, replaced by an isolation/plausibility self-test already run. Net -1 harness subsystem, cycle time -12s/pack.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part-count -HVIL harness, -2 poles per HV connector across the pack. Simpler connectors ease mating and cut cost. Poka-yoke shifts to electrical self-diagnosis rather than a physical loop that can be defeated by looping wire. Serviceability: service disconnect handled by voltage-detection lockout.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Deletes an entire redundant safety-wiring subsystem where electrical detection already exists
costSavingPotential.percentage: ~2–3% of LV BOM plus connector simplification
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: (€6–12 saved) × 100,000 = €0.6M–€1.2M; connector SKU simplification adds tooling savings

ideaData.riskNotes: This is the highest-scrutiny idea — HVIL is a widely-expected safety architecture. Reaction time to detect an opened live connector must beat the touch-safety window and be argued to ASIL-D per ISO 26262; must still meet ECE R100.03 and regional standards that may effectively mandate interlock behaviour. Mitigate by retaining a minimal HVIL on the service disconnect only, and proving electrical detection covers all other joints. Regulatory acceptance is the gating risk — confirm per market before deletion.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Tesla / high-integration BEV HV architectures minimising discrete interlock wiring — electrical HV-integrity monitoring reducing reliance on a full physical HVIL loop. How this differs: pushes toward software HVIL via isolation + continuity plausibility, deleting the dedicated interlock harness/pins legacy 800V packs thread through every connector, retaining only a service-disconnect interlock

ideaData.title: Single bidirectional contactor plus MOSFET soft-disconnect deletes second pole
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline Western 800V BDUs use two high-voltage DC contactors (main+ and main-, e.g. TE/Gigavac EV200-class 500A sealed gas-filled contactors ~€45 each) plus a separate precharge contactor and resistor. Proposal: retain one main mechanical contactor on the negative pole for galvanic isolation/HVIL compliance, and replace the positive-pole contactor with a normally-off SiC MOSFET half-bridge string (e.g. 1200V 20mΩ SiC in TO-247, 8-12 die paralleled to carry ~400A continuous) that performs make/break and precharge current-limiting in the same silicon. The MOSFET provides arc-less switching (no contact bounce, no gas-filled chamber), soft-start via gate ramp replacing the precharge resistor, and instant (<10µs) turn-off for fault current. Physics: SiC has 3× the critical field of Si, so a thin drift region gives low Rds(on) at 1200V; switching in the semiconductor eliminates the mechanical arc that forces DC contactors to be gas-filled and physically large.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes one €45 sealed DC contactor, the precharge contactor (€12) and precharge resistor+PCB (€6) per pack; the added SiC die (~€28) nets ~€35 saved per BDU. Removes one contactor coil driver channel and its diagnostic sense line from the BDU PCB, shrinking board area and one relay-weld failure mode from warranty.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: BDU busbar plane loses one large contactor footprint and its M8 stud terminations (2 fewer torqued joints per pack). SiC module reuses the existing thermal interface to the BDU baseplate. One fewer press-fit contactor station; adds one power-module solder/sinter reflow shared with existing SiC line. Net station count roughly flat, floor area down ~8%.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count -3 (contactor, precharge contactor, resistor) +1 SiC module. Two fewer M8 busbar joints removes a torque-verify + camera poka-yoke step. Serviceability: MOSFET is board-mounted not field-replaceable, but BDU already a sealed reman unit. Creepage to negative pole must be re-verified after layout compaction.

costSavingPotential.percentage: ~€35/pack net, ~0.3-0.5% of BDU-inclusive HV distribution cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: (€45 contactor + €12 precharge contactor + €6 resistor/PCB − €28 SiC die) × 100,000 = €35 × 100k = €3.5M

ideaData.riskNotes: SiC turn-off must clamp inductive HV bus overshoot below 1200V during fault interrupt — needs TVS/active clamp validated to ECE R100.03 isolation and short-circuit withstand. ideaData.title: Pyrofuse replaces melting fuse plus one main contactor
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: 800V BDU carries a bolt-in melting fuse (e.g. Bussmann/Littelfuse 500A aR semiconductor fuse ~€22) sized for slow overload PLUS two mechanical contactors that also serve as the crash-disconnect. Proposal: adopt a single pyrotechnic fuse (pyroswitch, e.g. Autoliv/Littelfuse PyroFuse-class, ~€18) with an integrated parallel melting element for slow overloads, triggered by the airbag ECU squib line for crash and by the BMS for fast DC fault. This lets the BDU drop from two contactors to one (negative pole for service isolation), because the crash-severance duty and fast-clearing duty are now handled by the pyro element severing the busbar in <2ms — far faster than a contactor can arc-quench at 800V DC. Physics: a pyro charge mechanically cuts the copper conductor and pushes the ends into an arc-splitting chamber with quartz sand, extinguishing an 800V/>10kA arc that a mechanical contactor cannot break; the passive melting element in parallel covers the low-multiple overload region where pyro would not self-trigger.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes one €45 main contactor and its coil driver; pyro replaces a €22 melting fuse for a €4 delta. Net ~€41/pack. Eliminates one contactor's HVIL and diagnostic channel and one busbar interruption joint, shrinking BDU busbar copper mass.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: BDU assembly loses one contactor press/torque station and gains one squib-connector insertion (shared with airbag harness process). Pyro is a sealed cartridge, torque-to-busbar only. Cycle time per BDU roughly neutral; scrap risk from contactor weld-check disappears. Requires ESD-controlled squib handling zone.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count -1 contactor, fuse swapped 1:1. One fewer 800V busbar break-and-reconnect. Squib connector is keyed/CPA poka-yoke to prevent mis-mate. Serviceability: pyro is single-shot — post-crash the whole BDU is replaced, aligned with reman-unit strategy; melting element covers benign overloads without triggering pyro (avoids false single-shot burns).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Consolidates crash-disconnect, fast-fault and overload protection while deleting a contactor
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: (€45 contactor − €4 pyro-vs-fuse delta) × 100,000 = €41 × 100k = €4.1M

ideaData.riskNotes: Pyro trigger logic must guarantee severance under crash per ECE R100.03 and the crash-disconnect requirement, AND must not false-fire (no-fire current threshold validated). Single mechanical pole means service isolation relies on one contactor — prove isolation resistance and lockout per GB 38031-2025. Squib storage/transport is a Class 1 explosive logistics constraint requiring UN certification.

How this differs: uses the pyro to also retire the crash-duty contactor and combines a passive melting element in parallel, rather than running pyro alongside two full contactors

ideaData.title: Laser-welded stamped busbar BDU replaces bolted copper bar stack
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline BDUs route HV between fuse, contactors and pack terminals with individually machined C110 copper bars (3-5mm thick) bolted at each interface with M8 studs, torqued and torque-verified — typically 8-12 bolted HV joints per BDU, each a contact-resistance and loosening risk. Proposal: a single stamped-and-formed C110 half-hard busbar carrier (one +bar, one −bar) with laser-welded stubs to the contactor/fuse terminals, insulated by an overmoulded PA66-GF30 frame that also provides creepage barriers and fixtures every component in one plane (a busbar-integrated BDU per Qilin/Blade practice). Contact interfaces are laser-welded (Cu-Cu conduction-mode weld) rather than bolted, giving a gas-tight, low-resistance joint. Physics: laser welds give ~2-4µΩ joint resistance vs 20-50µΩ for a bolted joint that relies on asperity contact and degrades with thermal cycling — lower I²R loss lets the same current run on ~15% less copper cross-section.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Copper cross-section reduced ~15% via lower joint resistance and shorter routing; deletes ~10 M8 bolts, washers and their torque/verify labour; overmoulded frame replaces separate insulators, spacers and brackets. Copper is the dominant BOM in a BDU, so a 15% copper-mass cut plus fastener/labour deletion dominates savings.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Replaces 8-12 bolted-joint torque stations with 8-12 laser-weld pulses on one welding cell (fast, shared with pack busbar welder). Overmould tool is new capex (~€300k) amortised over volume. Eliminates torque-audit and re-torque rework loop. Cycle time per BDU down ~25%.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count drops from ~20 loose bars/insulators/fasteners to ~3 (two busbars + one overmould). Welds are single-side access, laser-line-of-sight designed in. Tolerance stack collapses because components locate to the moulded frame. Serviceability trade: welded joints are not field-separable — matches sealed reman BDU strategy.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Cuts copper mass and eliminates the bolted-joint labour and reliability burden of the BDU
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: ~1.8kg Cu at €9/kg × 15% = €2.4 + €0.6 fasteners/labour = €30 gross − tooling amort €3/pack ≈ €28 × 100k

ideaData.riskNotes: Laser welds must pass vibration/thermal-cycle without crack propagation per ISO 12405-4 and maintain isolation/creepage clearances per ECE R100.03; overmould flash into creepage gaps is a scrap driver needing vision inspection. Weld porosity raises resistance/hotspot risk — inline resistance or thermography check required. Copper down-gauge must be validated against fault-current I²t heating before the fuse clears.

How this differs: applies the CTP busbar-integration and weld-not-bolt principle specifically to the BDU subassembly, which Western packs still bolt for serviceability

ideaData.title: Copper-alloy shunt busbar segment replaces discrete shunt resistor
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline BDU current sensing uses a discrete manganin/Isotan precision shunt resistor (e.g. 50-100µΩ, ~€8) bolted into the busbar with two extra Kelvin-sense joints, plus an isolated amplifier. Proposal: form the current-sense element directly into the main busbar by locally necking the C110 copper to a calibrated cross-section and laser-trimming it to a known milliohm-fraction resistance, with integrated Kelvin taps stamped from the same blank — a busbar-integrated shunt. Temperature compensation is done in firmware using copper's known +0.39%/°C TCR and a co-located NTC, rather than paying for a low-TCR alloy. Physics: copper's resistance is predictable and stable; a calibrated necked segment gives a repeatable µΩ drop, and firmware TCR correction recovers the accuracy that manganin buys with material cost. This keeps sensing in the busbar plane and deletes two bolted Kelvin interfaces.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −1 shunt, −2 Kelvin bolted joints. Sense taps are integral, eliminating tolerance stack between shunt and busbar. Laser-trim is single-side. Serviceability neutral (sealed BDU). Poka-yoke: each busbar carries its trimmed resistance value in a 2D code for firmware pairing.

Necked section is a mechanical/thermal weak point at fault current — validate I²t heating and vibration fatigue per ISO 12405-4 so it is not the unintended fusing point.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: both main contactors are specified as high-cost gas-filled (hydrogen-atmosphere) sealed DC contactors rated to make/break high fault current, because they must survive worst-case hot-switching and precharge inrush. Proposal: add a small solid-state precharge/soft-connect stage (a 1200V SiC MOSFET + gate ramp, ~€6) that guarantees the main contactors ALWAYS close and open into a soft (near-zero-di/dt, current-limited) condition, so the mechanical contactors never hot-switch. This lets both mains be downgraded from gas-filled hot-switch-rated contactors (~€45) to air-break economy sealed contactors rated only for cold-switching and continuous current (~€22). Physics: contactor cost is dominated by arc-interruption capability (gas fill, contact materials, chamber). If the SiC stage always establishes and collapses current before contacts move, the arc energy the mechanical contacts see is near zero, so a cheaper arc-rating suffices while galvanic isolation and continuous ampacity are unchanged.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Downgrades 2 contactors from €45 to €22 = €46 saved, minus €6 SiC precharge stage and €4 controls = net ~€36/pack. Also deletes the legacy precharge resistor (€3) whose duty is absorbed by the SiC ramp.

Emergency-open (crash) still needs a guaranteed break path (pyro or one hot-switch-capable contactor) per GB 38031-2025. Endurance of economy contactors under vibration per ISO 12405-4 must be re-proven.

ideaData.title: Aluminium busbars replace copper in BDU via cross-section upsize
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline BDU main busbars are C110 copper (~€9/kg, ~1.8kg per BDU) chosen for conductivity. Proposal: switch the high-current BDU busbars to EN AW-1350 or 6101-T6 aluminium (~€3/kg) with cross-section increased ~1.6× to compensate for aluminium's ~61% IACS conductivity, and use friction-stir or ultrasonic Al-Cu transition joints only at the unavoidable copper interfaces (contactor/fuse terminals). Aluminium is ~30% the density of copper per volume of conductivity-equivalent bar, so even at 1.6× cross-section the busbar is lighter and far cheaper. Where package allows the extra cross-section (the BDU has spare vertical room versus the cell stack), this is a direct material substitution. Physics: aluminium's lower conductivity is offset by more area; the I²R and mass trade favours Al when volume is available, and modern Al-Cu ultrasonic/FSW joints achieve <10µΩ transitions with proven durability.

Aluminium's lower fusing I²t means fault-current heating and the coordination with the fuse/pyro must be re-validated under GB 38031-2025 so busbars don't become the weak link.

ideaData.title: Multi-chamber crash extrusion sill deletes bolt-on crush box
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline Western 800V packs bolt a separate roll-formed or cast crush-box element inboard of the rocker to the tray perimeter frame with an AA6082-T6 extruded rail, forming a two-part load path with a bolted/adhered interface that must be sealed and inspected. Proposal: extrude the pack side-sill frame as a single AA6008-T6 (or 6082-T6 for higher strength) multi-chamber closed profile, 3–5 internal webs, wall 2.0–2.8 mm, forming the crash-energy-absorbing crush zone AND the tray perimeter in one part. The multi-chamber section folds progressively under lateral pole/side-impact loading, dissipating energy through controlled buckling of the inner webs rather than transferring it through a bolted joint. Section outer wall 3.0 mm, inner cell-side wall 2.0 mm keeps the cell-facing wall stiff enough to hold intrusion below the cell keep-out zone. This mirrors BYD Blade CTB and Tesla structural-pack practice where the sill IS the crash frame.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the separate crush-box stamping/casting (1 part), its ~14 M6 fasteners per side, the bolt-hole sealing, and one weld/adhesive interface. One extrusion replaces 2 subassemblies; fewer flanges to machine and seal; scrap falls because there is no bolted-joint rework.

Adds a longer extrusion press stroke and a 5-axis end-machining fixture per rail. Net stations down ~3; cycle time drops as bolt torquing sequence is deleted. Extrusion tooling capex ~€120k/profile vs €400k+ casting die.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −2/side, fastener count −28/pack. Tolerance stack collapses from a 3-part chain (crush box + bracket + rail) to a single extruded datum. Poka-yoke: asymmetric chamber cross-section prevents left/right mis-install. Serviceability: sill no longer separable, so side-impact damage means tray-frame replacement — acceptable at this structural level.

Weld-affected zone at rail ends must retain T6 properties; use post-weld artificial aging or friction-stir end closures.

ideaData.title: Continuous FIPG-in-groove seal cured on-line replaces EPDM cord
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline legacy packs (EVA2, Taycan-class) use a die-cut EPDM/silicone gasket cord or a pre-formed frame gasket placed by hand/robot into the lid flange, requiring inventory, splice joints and a placement station. Proposal: robotically dispense a formed-in-place gasket of a fast-cure two-component polyurethane or heat-cure silicone (e.g. shore-A 30–40, bead 4–5 mm) directly into a machined/extruded V-groove in the tray perimeter flange, with the bead profile controlling compression set. On lid assembly the FIPG compresses to ~50% and seals to IP67/IP6K9K. The physics: a continuous jointless bead removes the splice leak paths of a cut cord, and dispensing to the actual as-built groove geometry compensates for flange flatness variation that a fixed-section cord cannot. Cure-in-place before or after lid close depending on chemistry.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Eliminates gasket-cord piece cost, its splice scrap, and gasket inventory/logistics; deletes the manual/robot place-and-seat station. Dispense volume tracks groove length only — no offcut scrap. Yield rises from fewer seal leaks at splices.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Adds one mix-dispense robot cell (metering pump + static mixer) and a cure conveyor if heat-cure; deletes the gasket-place station and gasket kitting. Cycle ~30-60 s/perimeter, parallel to lid staging. Capex ~€250k dispenser vs recurring gasket piece cost; consumable is resin drum.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Removes 1 purchased part and its splice; joining access unchanged. Tolerance-tolerant: bead fills 0.3-0.5 mm flange gap variation a fixed cord cannot. Poka-yoke via vision-verified bead continuity. Serviceability: FIPG must be scraped and re-dispensed on reopen — acceptable for reman, worse than reusable cord, so pair with bolt-on lid variants only where reman is not required.

Ensure resin is halogen-free and non-corrosive to AA6xxx flange (no acetoxy silicones).

title: Tailor-rolled-blank steel cover panel with graded thickness
description: Removes ~15-25% of panel steel mass by deleting over-thickness in field zones; one TRB replaces a heavier single-gauge blank plus any local reinforcement patches (part-count −1 to −2 doublers). Fewer patch welds → less weld energy and scrap. Baseline: a stamped steel or aluminium cover/floor panel is a single-gauge blank (e.g. DC04 1.2 mm or AA5754 1.5 mm) sized to the most demanding zone, so most of the panel is over-thick. Proposal: use a tailor-rolled blank (TRB) of DP600 or DC04 with continuously varying thickness (e.g. 0.8 mm in low-load field zones tapering to 1.6 mm at flange/mount lands) produced by flexible rolling before stamping. Physics: bending stiffness scales with t³, so material is placed only where load demands it; the thick lands carry crash-mount and clamp loads while the thin field regions shed mass and cost. A single continuous blank avoids the weld lines of a tailor-welded blank, keeping the panel sealable and corrosion-continuous.

ideaData.title: Long-fibre SMC cover with moulded-in seal lip and EMC filler
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: an aluminium stamped cover plus a separate cut gasket plus a bonded copper-mesh or coating for EMC shielding — three functions, three parts, three process steps. Proposal: mould a single glass-fibre SMC (vinyl-ester, ~30-35% glass, 2.5-3.0 mm nominal) top cover that integrates (a) a moulded-in elastomer overmould seal lip along the flange, (b) a nickel/graphite-filled conductive gel-coat or embedded conductive veil on the inner face for EMC attenuation, and (c) moulded-in bolt-flange lands with compression limiters. Physics: SMC's low density (~1.9 g/cm³) and net-shape moulding let three parts collapse into one; the conductive inner layer provides a Faraday attenuation path (30-40 dB) sufficient for cover shielding without a metal skin; the overmould seal replaces the gasket. Non-structural cover — crash duty stays with the tray/sill.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Collapses 3 parts (cover + gasket + EMC screen) into 1 moulded part; deletes gasket place and EMC-mesh bond stations. Net-shape moulding removes stamping die and trim scrap. Mass down vs aluminium cover. Fewer fastener sealing points.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Adds a compression-mould SMC press with overmould insert; deletes stamping die + EMC-mesh application + gasket place stations. Cure ~90-150 s. Tooling capex ~€350-500k SMC tool vs stamping die ~€400k, offset by station deletions. Colour/UV cap on outer face if exposed.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part count −2 (gasket, EMC screen) and their process steps. Moulded compression limiters fix bolt clamp load (poka-yoke against over-torque crush). Tolerance held by tool; no TWB welds. Serviceability: bolted cover remains removable; overmould seal is reusable a few cycles.

ideaData.riskNotes: Must pass EMC (CISPR 25 / ECE R10 emissions & immunity) with the conductive layer, IP67 with the overmould lip, and flame-retardance for the vent-adjacent cover; risks are EMC attenuation shortfall and SMC creep at bolt lands — validate shielding-effectiveness sweep, compression-set on the lip, and clamp-load retention. Confirm SMC does not compromise thermal-propagation containment vs GB 38031-2025 (add liner if over cells).

ideaData.title: Shared standardised bolt-flange interface across pack family
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: each pack size in a range has a bespoke perimeter bolt pattern, flange width and mount-hole layout, driving unique fixtures, torque programs and body interfaces per variant. Proposal: define a single standardised bolt-flange interface geometry — fixed flange width (e.g. 22 mm), fixed bolt pitch (40 mm), common M8 fastener, common mount-pad positions on a shared datum grid — carried across the whole 800V pack family (short and long wheelbase, two energy sizes). The tray perimeter and lid flanges are extruded/formed to the same cross-section; only the tray length changes. Physics is commonisation, not mechanics: identical joint geometry lets one torque program, one seal cross-section, one sealing FIPG groove and one set of assembly fixtures serve all variants, amortising tooling and validation over higher volume.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Amortises fixture, torque-tool, seal-groove tooling and crash-joint validation across the whole family instead of per-variant; slashes unique-part count in fasteners, seal cords and mount hardware; cuts PPAP and validation spend per programme.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One flange-forming die/extrusion cross-section and one bolt-pattern drill/CNC program serve all variants → fewer die sets and faster changeover (SMED). Single assembly fixture family. Capex avoided on duplicate tooling; changeover time between variants drops sharply on a mixed line.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Fastener and seal SKUs collapse to one each. Common datum grid poka-yokes body/pack mating. Tolerance managed once. Serviceability improves — one service torque spec and one seal part number across the range.

ideaData.title: Cold-formed martensitic-steel sill insert bonded into Al frame
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: to hit side-pole intrusion targets, aluminium sill sections must be thick (2.5-3.0 mm, multi-chamber), consuming costly extrusion mass; all-steel sills are cheaper but heavy. Proposal: a hybrid — a thin cold-formed martensitic steel insert (e.g. MS1500, 1.0-1.2 mm, roll-formed hat) structurally bonded (crash epoxy) and mechanically clinched inside a lighter AA6008-T6 outer extrusion (walls reduced to 1.8-2.0 mm). Physics: martensitic steel's very high yield (~1200-1500 MPa) carries the intrusion barrier duty at minimal thickness, while the aluminium extrusion provides packaging, sealing surface and corrosion isolation. The composite section beats both a pure-Al thick section on cost and a pure-steel section on mass, exploiting each material where it is best per unit cost and per unit strength.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cheaper steel (~€1.0/kg) displaces expensive thick aluminium (~€3.2/kg) in the strength-critical wall, so total sill material cost falls even as the Al wall thins. High yield lets the insert be thin, limiting the mass penalty. One bonded assembly replaces an over-thick single extrusion.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Adds a roll-form line for the MS insert + a bond/clinch cell into the extrusion; the Al extrusion die is retooled thinner. Adhesive cure runs in-line. Net capex modest (roll-forming is cheap); offset by lighter extrusion press load and lower Al buy. Galvanic isolation adds a sealant step.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Two parts bonded vs one thick extrusion — part-count +1 but material cost down. Clinch/bond needs open-section access before closeout (design DFA: insert before end-caps). Poka-yoke via keyed insert length. Serviceability: sill is sacrificial in crash, replaced whole — no field disassembly of the hybrid.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Al wall thinned ~0.7 kg/m ×~3 m ×€3.2 = €6.7 saved − MS insert ~1.2 kg ×€1.0 = €1.2 add ⇒ net ~€5-8/m; ×~2 sills + tooling amort ⇒ €17-30/pack ×100,000 = €1.7M-€3.0M

Weld/HAZ avoided (bonded/clinched), preserving MS1500 martensite. Validate mixed-material crush FEA against physical pole test.

title: Mica-to-aerogel swap on lid-side propagation barrier
description: Mica board at ~€9–12/m2 material plus fragile handling/waste is replaced by die-cut aerogel-scrim at lower installed cost after scrap; areal mass drops ~1.5 kg/pack cutting warranty-relevant lid deflection and freeing energy budget. ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline Western 800V packs (Taycan J1, Audi PPE) protect the lid interior against runaway ejecta with a 2.0–2.5 mm rigid muscovite/phlogopite mica board (density ~2.0 g/cm3, ~0.35 W/mK) bonded to the underside of the stamped-aluminium lid. ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Deletes the tiled mica place-and-bond sub-station (mica cracks on handling, ~4–7% scrap); replaces with a single roll-fed die-cut and vacuum-pick lamination onto the lid. Cycle time drops ~15 s/lid. No brittle-board dunnage. One adhesive bead pass instead of per-tile beading.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Single flexible blanket conforms to lid ribs and bolt bosses, eliminating gap-fill between rigid mica tiles. Poka-yoke via asymmetric die-cut outline keying to lid studs. title: Two-component intumescent spray-coat cell-face barrier vs discrete pads
description: Deletes per-cell die-cut barrier parts (material + kerf scrap + placement labour) and the associated pick-place stations; coating is metered by mass so material use tracks exactly the coated area, cutting BOM and complexity of a multi-SKU pad inventory. Baseline packs place a discrete die-cut inter-cell barrier (0.3–0.5 mm mica sheet or aerogel pad) between every prismatic cell pair — dozens of placed parts per pack. Proposal: robotically spray a 0.8–1.2 mm two-component water-based intumescent coating (ammonium-polyphosphate/pentaerythritol/melamine char system in an acrylic binder) onto the broad face of every cell before stacking. At ~180–200 °C the coating expands 15–40× into a carbonaceous char foam (~0.05 W/mK), forming an in-situ insulating flame-stop exactly where a neighbouring cell vents. Below trigger it is a thin dielectric film adding negligible stack thickness, preserving volumetric efficiency and stack compression control.

title: Combined aerogel-mica hybrid barrier: aerogel bulk, mica hot-face
description: Downgauges expensive thick mica (0.3 mm vs 2.0 mm) and thick aerogel to the minimum each needs, cutting the dominant material cost; the laminate is a single placed part so no extra assembly labour vs a mono-material barrier. Baseline high-nickel packs over-spec a single-material barrier: either thick mica (heavy, moderate insulation) or thick aerogel (light but abrades and can spall under a direct 1100 °C flame jet). Proposal: a laminated hybrid barrier — 0.3 mm phlogopite mica hot-face bonded to a 2.5 mm aerogel-scrim core, total 2.8 mm. The mica takes the direct flame/particle erosion (melting point >1200 °C, no spall) while the low-conductivity aerogel does the bulk thermal-gradient work behind it. This exploits each material where it wins: mica for ablation/erosion resistance, aerogel for insulation-per-mm and mass. Used on cell-face and lid positions adjacent to NCM811 rows where the ejecta is hottest.

title: Ceramic-forming silicone intumescent replaces mica on tray floor shelf
description: Combines two subassembly functions — bottom fire barrier and cell-bottom cushion/gap-fill — into one sprayed coating, deleting one placed part class and its stations; coating meters to area cutting die-cut scrap; protects tray so a thinner/cheaper tray floor is possible. Baseline packs bond a mica board or ceramic-fibre mat onto the tray floor 'shelf' under cell bottoms to protect the tray from bottom-vented ejecta (relevant to cell-inversion / bottom-vent architectures). Proposal: apply a 1.5–2 mm ceramifiable silicone coating (silicone binder loaded with mica flake + low-melting glass frit + wollastonite). Below ~400 °C it is a flexible elastomer that also acts as tolerance-absorbing cell-bottom cushion; above ~600 °C the frit sinters the filler into a self-supporting rigid ceramic that insulates and blocks the ejecta from eroding the aluminium tray. It combines the runaway barrier and the cell-bottom gap-pad/cushion into one sprayed layer.

title: Aerogel only over high-nickel rows, thin film elsewhere zoning
description: Removes expensive aerogel from the majority of gaps that do not need it, converting them to a cheap thin film; total aerogel area per pack falls sharply while worst-case rows keep full protection — pure material-cost reduction with no safety loss where it matters. Baseline packs apply a uniform 2–3 mm aerogel or mica barrier across ALL inter-cell gaps regardless of cell chemistry or thermal exposure. In dual-chemistry / high-nickel packs the propagation energy is highly non-uniform. Proposal: risk-map the array — full 3 mm aerogel-scrim inter-cell barriers only across the NCM811 high-nickel rows and edge/hotspot cells (highest onset energy and jet velocity), and a thin 0.3 mm PPS-film dielectric spacer across cooler LFP or low-stress interior positions where propagation margin already exists. Barrier thickness is matched to local calorimetric runaway energy rather than the worst-case cell applied everywhere.

title: Roll-fed mica-paper vent liner replaces rigid mica board in duct
description: Substitutes low-cost flexible mica paper for high-cost rigid mica board in positions where structural rigidity isn't needed; roll-fed die-cut cuts the 4–7% brittle-board breakage scrap to near zero and speeds application, lowering both material and labour. Baseline vent-duct and lid ejecta liners use rigid pressed mica board (2–3 mm, resin-bonded muscovite) that is expensive per kg, brittle, and cut with high kerf waste. Proposal: switch the non-structural liner positions to flexible calendered mica paper (0.5–1.0 mm, unbonded or minimally-bonded muscovite film) laminated to a thin steel or aluminium carrier only where the liner sees the ejecta jet. title: Self-draining sill channel with one-way duckbill deletes drain plugs
description: Deletes manual drain plugs and their sealing/torque, downsizes desiccant packs (moisture now self-clears), and reduces breathing-membrane spec (no condensation-load driver). ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: overcurrent protection between cell groups uses discrete bolted or welded fuse elements — bought parts at €4–12 each with housings and two joints apiece; a large pack carries 4–12 of them, each adding resistance, mass and two potential failure interfaces. Proposal: form the fuse function into the busbar itself — a calibrated reduced-section neck (waterjet- or stamp-profiled, with arc-quenching silica-filled ceramic sleeve clipped over the neck) engineered to the same time-current characteristic as the discrete fuse, following the fusible-link practice BYD applies inside Blade pack bussing and Tesla applies at cell level with bond wires. ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: LFP (LiFePO4) blade/prismatic cathode at ~150-170 mAh/g, 3.2V nominal, giving ~160 Wh/kg pack (Qilin LFP / Blade level). Proposal: substitute LMFP (LiMn0.6Fe0.4PO4) cathode delivering a second voltage plateau at ~4.1V (Mn3+/Mn2+) in addition to the 3.4V Fe plateau, raising average cell voltage from ~3.2V to ~3.7V at near-identical specific capacity (~150 mAh/g). Energy = capacity × voltage, so ~15% cell-level Wh/kg uplift at the same coating thickness, foil, separator and can. Mn is cheaper per kg than the marginal Ni/Co it displaces versus climbing to NMC. The olivine PO4 framework retains LFP's thermal stability (no O2 release below ~250°C). Requires carbon-coated nano-LMFP and a blended (10-20% LFP) buffer to counter Mn Jahn-Teller distortion and Mn dissolution; electrolyte gets a Mn-trapping additive (e.g. 1% LiDFOB).

title: Blended Si-C anode at 8% dose lifts capacity, keeps swelling manageable
description: Higher anode capacity lets same can hold more kWh → €/kWh drops as inactive mass (Cu foil, can, separator) amortises over more energy; fewer cells per pack cut interconnect and busbar cost. Proposal: blend 8 wt% silicon-carbon composite (SiOx or Si/C nanocomposite, ~1500-2000 mAh/g) into graphite, raising anode capacity to ~500 mAh/g. title: Laser-notched multi-tab electrode replaces single stamped tab
description: Deletes progressive stamping die (tooling + maintenance + changeover), removes discrete tab-weld stations, cuts scrap from tab misalignment. Lower DCR reduces derating so fewer/less cells needed for a fast-charge spec, and eases cooling. Baseline: single (or few) stamped Al/Cu tab per electrode with a punch die, common in legacy prismatic/pouch cells, forcing current to travel the full electrode length → high in-cell resistance and hotspots limiting fast charge. Proposal: fibre-laser-notch a continuous multi-tab (comb) pattern directly on the coated foil edge, giving many parallel current paths (tabless-like) that cut internal resistance and electrode thermal gradient. Lower DCR means less I2R heat at 4C-6C, enabling higher fast-charge power without cell derating and improving round-trip efficiency. It also removes stamping dies (die wear, changeover, scrap) and eliminates tab-welding of discrete tabs. At 800V the reduced DCR lowers pack heat load, shrinking cooling demand marginally.

title: Nickel-plated DC04 deep-drawn steel can replaces AA3003 prismatic housing
description: Material substitution: can mass falls ~45% while €/kg falls ~65%, so can cost drops ~€0.55–0.85 per cell; compression plates and tie-rods downsize because the can carries stack load; laser-weld cap seam parameters transfer from proven cylindrical lines. Baseline: prismatic cell housings deep-drawn or impact-extruded from AA3003-H14 aluminium at 0.6–0.8 mm wall, laser-welded to an aluminium cap plate. Proposal: pre-nickel-plated DC04 deep-drawing steel at 0.30–0.40 mm wall, drawn on the same transfer-press class Tesla uses for 4680 cans. Steel's ~3× yield strength over AA3003 lets the wall thin by ~45% while raising internal-pressure burst margin, and steel strip at ~€0.9/kg vs aluminium sheet at ~€3.2/kg cuts can material cost even after plating. The higher elastic modulus also stiffens the cell stack against pouch-like bulging, allowing lighter module compression hardware. Nickel plating (2–4 µm, strip-plated before forming) provides corrosion resistance and a weldable terminal surfac

Mitigation: coined score line re-tuned for steel ductility with heater-trigger vent tests.

title: Coined can-bottom score vent deletes separate burst-disc assembly
description: Deletes one part (disc), one laser weld, one leak-test station and its scrap stream; coining is a marginal die action inside an existing press stroke. Saving ~€0.30–0.45/cell plus 0.8 s cycle at the cap line. Baseline: prismatic caps carry a separate welded burst disc — a stamped AA1050 membrane laser-welded over a cap aperture, plus its leak-test station. title: Z-fold stacked electrode replaces jelly-roll winding in long prismatic LFP

title: Cu–Al clad transition plate replaces friction-welded terminal stud

Baseline: prismatic cell negative terminals bridge copper (cell-internal collector) to aluminium (pack busbar) via a friction-welded or ultrasonically-welded Cu/Al stud assembly — a five-piece stack with two dissimilar-metal welds made cell-by-cell. title: Rib-rolled 0.4 mm can wall replaces plain 0.6 mm prismatic wall
description: Aluminium mass per can falls ~30% (≈90–140 g), worth €0.30–0.45/cell at sheet prices; stiffer faces let module compression plates downgauge 15%; TIM void scrap falls at pack line. Baseline: prismatic aluminium cans at 0.6–0.8 mm constant wall, sized by panel breathing (electrode swelling pressure up to 0.3 MPa) and handling stiffness, not by burst. Proposal: roll longitudinal micro-ribs (0.8 mm pitch, 0.15 mm depth) into the two large can faces during strip feed, then draw at 0.40 mm wall. The ribs raise the face's flexural section modulus ~2.1×, so breathing deflection at end-of-life swelling stays under the 0.5 mm module clearance despite the thinner gauge. Material per can falls ~30%. The ribbed texture also creates micro-channels that improve gap-filler wet-out on the cooled face, shaving TIM void rate. Same die concept Tesla applies to structural panels; here it is applied at can scale on the existing draw line with a textured roll pass ahead of the blanking press.

title: Integrated stamped cap: fill port, vent seat and terminal towers one piece
description: Part consolidation 8–12 → 4 pieces deletes three joining operations and two sealing interfaces per cell; machining is replaced by progressive stamping at one-third the piece price; fewer interfaces cut He-leak failure rate. Baseline: a prismatic cap assembly is 8–12 pieces — machined cap plate, separate fill-port bung, welded vent-disc seat ring, two terminal towers with sub-gaskets, plus rivets. Proposal: a single progressive-die stamped cap in AA5052-H32 (1.2 mm) that forms the fill-port chimney, the vent seat counterbore and both terminal-tower pockets as drawn features in one strip pass, following the part-integration logic BYD applies to Blade caps. Machined-plate flatness is replaced by coined sealing lands (±0.02 mm local flatness at gasket zones only — the rest of the cap is allowed to be a stamping). Piece count falls to 4 (cap + 2 terminal inserts + fill ball), assembly welds fall from 5 to 2, and the machined cap's ~€1.10 cost falls to ~€0.45 stamped.

title: Selective shear-zone potting cuts structural foam mass by half
description: Structural PU is €6–9/kg: halving 12 kg saves €36–54/pack; dispense time falls ~40% releasing robot capacity; lower exotherm cuts cure distortion rework on the pack top plane. Baseline: Tesla-style structural packs pot the full cell array in polyurethane structural foam — ~9–14 kg of two-part PU per pack — although FEA shows shear transfer between cells and face sheets concentrates along the outer two cell rows and above cross-member lines; the mid-field foam works at <20% of its allowable. ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: serviceable power-electronics interfaces inside the pack (BDU semiconductors, contactor plates, DC-DC modules) use thermal grease — pump-out and dry-out over thermal cycling are the known degradation modes, driving conservative derating and a smear-quality dependence on operator technique; every service intervention demands clean-and-reapply with contamination risk in the field. Proposal: 200–250 µm phase-change material (PCM) sheets (45–55 °C softening, 3–5 W/mK) die-cut to each footprint: solid at room temperature (clean handling, zero technique dependence, position verified by vision), flowing at first operational heat-up to wet the interface like grease without its migration. PCM sheets survive 1,000+ thermal cycles with <10% resistance drift versus grease's typical 30–50%, and service becomes peel-and-replace with no cleaning step. Power-module suppliers (Infineon application notes) already sanction PCM for exactly this duty.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes grease-application technique scrap and its QA burden; derating margin held for grease dry-out is recovered as either smaller heatsink mass or higher rated current; field-service time per intervention drops ~15 min with no contamination escapes.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Sheet placement joins the existing film pick-and-place; grease dispense/smear station deleted. Incoming QC: softening point + thickness sampling. Service kits simplify to labelled die-cuts.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Solid-at-assembly TIM is position-verifiable (grease is not) — a QA capability upgrade; peel-and-replace serviceability with zero cleaning aligns with dealer skill reality. One SKU per footprint, but footprints already exist as grease stencils.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Thermal quality stops depending on smear technique; dry-out margin returns as rating or mass.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: QA/scrap credit + 15 min × service-event rate × labour rate + heatsink mass trim ~€1.5/pack

ideaData.riskNotes: First-melt voiding must be characterised (clamp pressure ≥0.3 MPa during first heat ensures wet-out — guaranteed by existing mounting springs); vertical-surface retention over life verified at 105 °C sustained; low-temperature start behaviour (pre-melt resistance) checked against cold-start current limits. Aged interface audited at teardown milestones.

title: Hollow glass microspheres cut gap-filler density 25% at grade
description: Cost per applied litre falls 10–18% (spheres are cheaper than displaced formulation mass); pack mass −1.4 kg is worth range or content elsewhere; freight and handling of TIM drums lightens proportionally. Baseline: gap fillers are dense (2.5–3.2 g/cm³) because thermal percolation is built with heavy alumina; a 6 kg TIM load contributes real pack mass, and material is bought by the kilogram — density is cost. Proposal: co-formulated fillers where 8–15 vol% hollow borosilicate glass microspheres (0.3–0.6 g/cm³, 20–50 µm) displace matrix polymer and part of the non-percolating filler fraction, cutting cured density to 1.9–2.3 g/cm³ at equal 2.0 W/mK class conductivity — sphere loading sits below the percolation-disruption threshold, and formulators (Momentive, Wacker publish such systems) balance the alumina network around them. Per-pack TIM mass falls ~1.4 kg (a direct Wh/kg credit) and per-litre applied cost falls ~10–18% because dispensed volume, not mass, is what the interface needs.

ideaData.title: Spacer-bead-dosed gap filler self-sets bond-line thickness
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: minimum TIM bond-line thickness under cells and cold-plate interfaces is guaranteed by machined stand-off bosses, stamped dimples or placed shims — features that cost machining passes or discrete parts, and that still let the bond line vary with clamp force and flatness stack, so the TIM layer is specified thicker than the thermal path needs (tolerance bought as material). Proposal: dose the gap filler itself with 1–2 wt% monodisperse spacer beads — soda-lime or polymer spheres at exactly the target bond line (e.g. 500 µm ±20 µm) — the die-attach and LCD-assembly technique that turns bond-line thickness into a material property: under placement force the interface closes onto the beads and stops, everywhere, regardless of local flatness or clamp scatter. Stand-off machining and shim parts are deleted, TIM nominal thickness drops to the bead diameter plus wet-out margin (−20–30% volume), and thermal resistance scatter across the pack tightens because every cell sits at the same gap.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Filler supplier pre-doses beads (no line change); placement press force window widens (force lands on beads, not on a tolerance calculation); stand-off machining stations or shim feeders deleted. ideaData.dfmDfa: Removes machined features and shim parts from trays/plates; assembly becomes force-insensitive within the press window — a robustness gain; bead diameter is a purchased property, so design changes to bond line are a material-order change, not a tooling change.

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: LV harness and sense-lead pass-throughs in module covers and internal walls use separate EPDM grommets — dozens of small parts pressed by hand into apertures, each a potential missed-seal or half-seated defect found only at pack leak test; grommet part numbers multiply with every harness revision. ideaData.title: Qualified closed-loop regrind quota cuts pack moulding resin buy
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: interior pack mouldings — cell holders, busbar carriers, LV brackets, covers in PP-GF/PA66-GF — are specified 100% virgin resin, while the moulding process itself generates 15–25% clean runner/sprue regrind that is sold off as scrap at a fraction of resin price; EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 direction on recycled content makes this a compliance asset being thrown away. Proposal: qualify a controlled closed-loop regrind quota — 20–30% in-house regrind blended into the same part families it came from (closed loop, so contamination and polymer history are known), with per-lot MFI and glass-length monitoring as the acceptance gate; glass-fibre attrition in one regrind cycle typically costs 5–10% of tensile properties, absorbed by the parts' existing margins at these quotas for non-creep-critical positions. The duty map marks which parts accept the quota (holders, covers, non-torqued brackets) and which stay virgin (creep- and HV-critical). Resin buy for the mapped family falls ~20% at essentially zero process cost — the granulator and dosing units are standard moulding-shop equipment.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Virgin resin purchases fall by the quota on mapped parts (20–30% of 3–5 kg/pack polymer): €4–9/pack; runner scrap revenue loss is far below virgin price avoided; recycled-content declarations for EU Battery Regulation reporting come free with the loop.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Granulator + gravimetric dosing at the moulder (standard kit, often already present); per-lot MFI/glass-length QC added; traceability records regrind ratio per batch — the same records the battery passport wants. No cycle-time or tooling change at validated quotas.
ideaData.dfmDfa: No geometry or assembly change; the duty map (which parts accept regrind) is the governance artefact — bound into drawings so a future part can't silently inherit a quota its duty forbids; dosing is machine-controlled, not operator judgement.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: The moulding shop's own scrap replaces a fifth of its resin buy, and the battery passport gets its recycled-content line for free.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 4 kg polymer × 25% quota × €3.2/kg virgin−scrap delta × 100k packs, less QC cost

ideaData.riskNotes: Property fade at the quota must be verified per part family (tensile, impact, V-0 retention on aged regrind blends — flame retardants can degrade with reprocessing, so FR grades get their own qualification); colour drift managed by masterbatch; quota capped and audited per lot. Any V-0 failure at quota keeps that family virgin — the map records the refusal, not silence.

ideaData.title: Pyrofuse plus HVIL strategy deletes the manual service disconnect
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: packs carry a manual service disconnect (MSD) — an orange lever-plug at €12–25 with its housing aperture, sealing, HV connector body and a lid cut-out — originating from first-responder and service doctrines of the 400V era; the MSD is also a chronic ingress and connector-wear warranty item. Proposal: delete the MSD, assigning its functions to parts the 800V pack already carries: a pyrotechnic disconnect (pyrofuse, standard for crash isolation on 800V platforms) provides emergency separation triggered electrically, first-responder isolation is provided by the cut-loop tab standardised in rescue sheets, and service isolation is achieved by the contactors plus a lockout-tagout LV interlock (HVIL loop with a keyed plug at the LV connector — a €1.5 part). Most new Chinese 800V packs and several European programmes have already shipped MSD-less; the deletion removes a sealed HV aperture — one fewer leak path and crash-intrusion consideration in the lid.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the MSD part (€12–25), its lid aperture machining and sealing, connector counterpart and assembly/test steps; removes an IP67 leak-test failure mode and an ingress warranty line; the pyrofuse and HVIL already exist — reassignment costs one keyed LV plug.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Lid tooling simplifies (no aperture); leak-test failure catalogue shrinks; EOL test replaces MSD-pull verification with HVIL-open + contactor-open verification (software). Service procedures rewritten around lockout-tagout — training content, not hardware.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part, aperture, seal and two assembly operations deleted; the lid becomes a simpler stamping/casting; service isolation becomes a procedure with a keyed part — poka-yoke by the HVIL loop refusing closure with the key absent.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: A 400V-era part, its hole, its seal and its failure modes leave a pack that already owns the safer answers.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: (MSD €12–25 + aperture/seal €3–5 + test time) × 100k + ingress-warranty credit

ideaData.riskNotes: Regulatory and market acceptance is the gate: ECE R100 and GB 18384 permit MSD-less designs when isolation is otherwise ensured, but specific-market service regulations and OEM rescue-sheet commitments must be re-verified; dealer lockout-tagout compliance audited. Pyrofuse single-use economics (replacement after trigger) priced into crash-repair strategy — stated openly.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: XPeng SEPA 2.0 (G6/G9) — MSD-less 800V pack doctrine using pyrofuse + contactor + HVIL layering. How this differs: packages the deletion for programmes with legacy service doctrines by pairing it with an explicit keyed-HVIL lockout part and rescue-sheet alignment, rather than assuming the doctrine shift

title: Aluminium busbars with clad copper terminals replace full-copper runs
description: Material substitution on the runs (Cu → Al at equal resistance) saves €25–45/pack at current metal prices; weight −2.5–4 kg; copper price-volatility exposure shrinks to the clad patches; forming and laser welding of Al are faster and cheaper than heavy Cu sections. Baseline: pack HV distribution often stays full copper (Cu-ETP) by habit — copper at ~€9–11/kg against aluminium's ~€2.6–3.0/kg, with the 800V transition already having halved current (and thus conductor cross-section) versus 400V equivalents; the remaining copper argument is contact-interface behaviour at terminals, not the run itself. Proposal: EN AW-6101-T6 aluminium busbars sized at the 1.6× cross-section that equalises resistance (still ~50% lighter and ~65% cheaper per conductor), with roll-bonded copper cladding ONLY at contact/terminal zones — the clad patch delivers copper's contact physics (no creep-driven joint relaxation, standard plating) exactly where surfaces mate, while the run between terminals is aluminium.

Clad-patch busbar strip is an established product (Wickeder/Materion class). At a large 800V pack's 6–9 kg copper bussing, conversion takes out 55–65% of conductor spend.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Material substitution on the runs (Cu → Al at equal resistance) saves €25–45/pack at current metal prices; weight −2.5–4 kg; copper price-volatility exposure shrinks to the clad patches; forming and laser welding of Al are faster and cheaper than heavy Cu sections.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Busbar supplier switches to clad-strip stamping/forming — same press class; bending radii re-checked for 6101-T6; laser welding parameters move to Al settings (established). Plating line load falls (only patches plate).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Same joint interfaces as today at the terminals (clad face is copper — downstream torque specs and platings unchanged); larger Al sections need routing-clearance review; lighter bars ease manual/robot handling at assembly.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Copper stays only as a few square centimetres of contact surface; the metres in between become aluminium.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 6–9 kg Cu → Al conversion at €5.5–6.5/kg net delta after upsizing, ×100k

ideaData.riskNotes: Galvanic and creep behaviour at Al-to-clad transitions is internal to the strip (metallurgical bond, no serviceable interface) — validated by thermal cycling −40/+105 ×1,000 with resistance drift <5%; clearance/creepage re-checked for the larger sections; fault-current (short-circuit) thermal transient re-calculated for Al's lower heat capacity per resistance — sections verified against the pack's protection curve.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Lucid Air / Gravity (Wunderbox) — voltage-driven conductor economy — high system voltage shrinking conductor duty. How this differs: converts the remaining habit-copper to aluminium with clad copper contact patches, keeping copper only as a surface where its contact physics is actually used

title: Observer-model thermistor rationing: eight sensors where twenty-four sat

ideaData.title: Observer-model thermistor rationing: eight sensors where twenty-four sat
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: packs carry 20–40 NTC thermistors glued or clipped across cells and busbars — each a part, a wire pair or sense-line channel, an ADC input and a connector pin; most were placed by early-programme caution, and fleet data shows high mutual correlation (adjacent-sensor correlation >0.97 in steady operation) — the array measures the same field many times. Proposal: reduce to 6–10 sensors placed by observability analysis (the thermal model identifies the minimum sensor set that reconstructs the full cell-temperature field within ±1.5 °C), with a Kalman-style observer in BMS software estimating unmeasured positions from the retained sensors plus current/coolant states — the approach BMW's energy-master architecture and most zonal BMS designs already use to cut sense channels. Each deleted NTC removes ~€0.35 of part+wire+pin plus its assembly and its connector-pin failure mode; the observer is software on the existing MCU.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: 16–30 sensor channels deleted at ~€0.35 all-in each plus assembly seconds; connector pin-count drops one size class on two housings; harness mass and routing complexity fall; field failures of sensor bonds (a real warranty line) shrink proportionally to population.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Fewer placement/bond operations and fewer EOL sensor checks; BMS software gains the observer with its validation suite. Harness and connector part numbers respin once. Thermal-model maintenance becomes a governed deliverable (the observer is only as honest as the model).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Part-count and connector-complexity reduction; remaining sensors sit at analytically chosen, access-friendly positions; DFMEA swaps many bond-failure lines for one observer-integrity line with plausibility diagnostics (sensor-disagreement monitoring).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: The pack was measuring one temperature field two dozen times; software keeps the information, hardware keeps eight probes.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 20 channels avg × €0.35 × 100k + assembly/test time + bond-failure warranty credit

ideaData.riskNotes: Observer must prove coverage in abuse corners (DCFC soak, cold start, cell-imbalance heating) — validated against a fully instrumented reference pack across the duty matrix; regulatory thermal-monitoring expectations (GB 38031-2025 early-warning) met by demonstrating estimated-field fidelity; plausibility diagnostics detect a failed retained sensor and widen margins gracefully — the degraded mode is defined, not assumed away.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: BMW Gen6 / Neue Klasse — observer-based thermal estimation reducing physical sense channels in the distributed BMS. How this differs: applies the sensor-observability ration to legacy-architecture packs whose NTC populations grew by caution, using their own fleet correlation data as the deletion evidence

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: HV lines crossing the pack boundary (to OBC, DC-DC, compressor) each use a two-part HV connector pair — plug and header at €18–45 per circuit, orange housings, CPA/HVIL features, and the pack-side pigtail that adds a crimp and a seal; three auxiliary circuits cost six connector halves and their assembly. Connector count per pack falls from 6–8 halves to 2 (one moulded header + one mating plug); the header's overmoulded construction eliminates individual wire seals (the chronic IP67 failure at HV connectors). Chinese 800V packs increasingly ship exactly this consolidation; connector suppliers offer application-specific moulded headers at volumes above ~60k/yr.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes 4–6 connector halves (€12–30 each with seals/CPA) and their crimp+assembly operations, replaced by one moulded header (~€22–35); leak-test failures at wire seals drop with the seal count; outboard harness side simplifies to one mate.

ideaData.dfmDfa: One mating action where three were (assembly and service both faster); keyed multi-way header is self-poka-yoke; aperture count reduction simplifies sealing and crash zoning of the pack wall.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Three sealed holes and six connector halves become one engineered interface.

Service replacement of one circuit means header replacement — priced and stated.

title: Selective silver plating shrinks to contact spots by masked plating
description: Silver mass per pack falls 60–80% (10–28 g → €8–28/pack at silver prices); plating line throughput rises (smaller plated area per part); precious-metal price exposure and PGM-style accounting burden shrink proportionally. Baseline: busbar and terminal contact surfaces are silver- or silver-graphite plated for low, stable contact resistance — but plating drawings habitually call full-face or full-end plating, so 5–20× the functional contact area carries silver at €0.8–1.2/g; a large pack's plated set can carry 15–35 g of silver where 3–6 g touches anything. Proposal: masked selective plating (brush/spot plating or masked rack plating) restricted to the actual contact footprints defined by joint analysis — the pressed-contact ellipse under each bolt plus a placement tolerance band; the rest of the bar keeps bare or tin flash. ideaData.title: Selective silver plating shrinks to contact spots by masked plating
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: busbar and terminal contact surfaces are silver- or silver-graphite plated for low, stable contact resistance — but plating drawings habitually call full-face or full-end plating, so 5–20× the functional contact area carries silver at €0.8–1.2/g; a large pack's plated set can carry 15–35 g of silver where 3–6 g touches anything. Proposal: masked selective plating (brush/spot plating or masked rack plating) restricted to the actual contact footprints defined by joint analysis — the pressed-contact ellipse under each bolt plus a placement tolerance band; the rest of the bar keeps bare or tin flash. Connector-industry economics has run selective plating for decades precisely because precious-metal area is the cost; busbar suppliers offer the same processes. Contact resistance and durability are unchanged where metal meets metal — the deleted silver never carried current.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Silver mass per pack falls 60–80% (10–28 g → €8–28/pack at silver prices); plating line throughput rises (smaller plated area per part); precious-metal price exposure and PGM-style accounting burden shrink proportionally.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Plating supplier adds masking tooling (reusable rubber/epoxy masks, ~€8–15k per part family); QA adds plated-footprint position check (vision) to thickness sampling. No pack-line change at all.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Zero geometry or assembly change; plated-spot position tolerance must cover joint-position tolerance stack — verified in the joint drawing chain; visual contrast of plated spots aids automated joint-position verification (a small QA bonus).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Most of the silver never carried current; the mask keeps the physics and returns the metal.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 15 g avg silver deletion × €0.9/g × 100k + plating-throughput credit − mask tooling

ideaData.riskNotes: Contact footprint definition must include worst-case bolt-position tolerance and re-torque scatter — footprint sized by contact-mechanics calculation with margin band; corrosion at bare/plated boundaries in humid cycling verified (85/85 1,000 h + mixed flowing gas test); any joint redesign re-triggers footprint review via drawing linkage.

title: Zonal ring harness replaces star-topology LV wiring inside the pack
description: Wire length −50–70% and connectors −60% (≈€8–16/pack material); harness assembly converts from manual loom-board work to robot-layable channel routing (labour −3–5 min/pack); harness SKU complexity and its change-management overhead shrink. Baseline: pack-internal LV wiring runs star topology — every CSC/sensor cluster wires individually back to the BMS master, producing 30–80 m of wire, multi-branch looms with 8–20 connectors, hand-taped breakouts and a harness that is the least automatable part in the pack. ideaData.title: Zonal ring harness replaces star-topology LV wiring inside the pack
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: pack-internal LV wiring runs star topology — every CSC/sensor cluster wires individually back to the BMS master, producing 30–80 m of wire, multi-branch looms with 8–20 connectors, hand-taped breakouts and a harness that is the least automatable part in the pack. Proposal: restructure to a zonal ring/daisy-chain — a single twisted-pair or CAN-FD/isoSPI ring visits each cell-supervision node in sequence (the architecture wireless-BMS designs emulate in RF), cutting wire length 50–70% and connector count to 4–6; nodes tap the ring via insulation-displacement or board-to-board links. XPeng's X-EEA zonal philosophy and BMW's distributed supervision both exploit topology to delete copper and connectors; inside the pack the same lever is available without radio. The ring routes along one moulded channel in the carrier — a straight, robot-layable path replacing the hand-formed loom octopus.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Wire length −50–70% and connectors −60% (≈€8–16/pack material); harness assembly converts from manual loom-board work to robot-layable channel routing (labour −3–5 min/pack); harness SKU complexity and its change-management overhead shrink.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Carrier moulding gains a routing channel (die feature); harness supplier retools to simple ring sections; BMS comms firmware handles ring addressing (existing isoSPI/CAN-FD stacks support it). EOL test simplifies: one ring continuity + node enumeration replaces branch-by-branch checks.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Fewer connectors and a deterministic path — automatable routing; node addressing auto-enumerates (no position-coded connectors to mismatch); service diagnosis improves (ring integrity check localises faults by node index).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: The loom octopus becomes one robot-laid ring; copper, connectors and hand labour leave together.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: (wire+connector €12 avg + 4 min labour)/pack × 100k − firmware/validation amortised

ideaData.riskNotes: Ring topology's single-break vulnerability handled by dual-direction communication (standard in isoSPI daisy chains — break localised, both segments still reached); EMC of the ring near HV busbars verified by routing separation rules and twisted-pair spec per CISPR 25; connector-count reduction must not orphan service disconnection points needed by repair strategy — checked against the repair map.

title: Tin-over-nickel replaces silver plating on static welded interfaces
description: Silver area re-specified to Sn/Ni at ~15% of plating cost across 40–70% of the plated set (€5–15/pack); plating-line silver inventory and its security/accounting overhead shrink; no capex anywhere — the saving is a specification correction. Baseline: plating specs frequently call silver on busbar surfaces that end up laser-welded, not pressed — a spec inherited from when every joint was bolted; on a welded interface the plating is consumed or bypassed by the weld nugget, so silver (€0.8–1.2/g) is bought to be vaporised. ideaData.title: Tin-over-nickel replaces silver plating on static welded interfaces
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: plating specs frequently call silver on busbar surfaces that end up laser-welded, not pressed — a spec inherited from when every joint was bolted; on a welded interface the plating is consumed or bypassed by the weld nugget, so silver (€0.8–1.2/g) is bought to be vaporised. Proposal: audit the joint map and re-specify all weld-destined surfaces to tin-over-nickel (Sn 3–6 µm over Ni 2 µm, ~15% of silver's cost) or bare aluminium with pre-weld laser cleaning; silver remains only on pressed, separable contacts where its anti-fretting and low film resistance earn the price. On mixed packs this typically re-specifies 40–70% of previously silvered area. Tin's solderability also aids the few brazed/sense-tab attachments, and nickel under-plate keeps corrosion behaviour at cut edges equivalent. This is a drawings-and-audit exercise: no geometry, tooling or process change at the pack line at all.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Silver area re-specified to Sn/Ni at ~15% of plating cost across 40–70% of the plated set (€5–15/pack); plating-line silver inventory and its security/accounting overhead shrink; no capex anywhere — the saving is a specification correction.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Plating suppliers re-rack for the revised spec; incoming QC updates plating maps. Weld parameters verified on Sn/Ni surfaces (tin's low boiling point demands weld-zone masking or pre-weld dezincing checks — parameters exist from busbar suppliers).
ideaData.dfmDfa: Zero assembly change; plating maps on drawings become joint-type-driven (welded vs pressed) — a governance improvement that survives future joint changes because the rule, not the instance, is documented.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Silver was being specified onto surfaces the laser vaporises; the drawing audit returns it.
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €5–15/pack plating delta × 100k; zero capex, audit labour one-time

ideaData.riskNotes: Tin near weld zones can contaminate the nugget — masked plating windows or bare-with-laser-clean zones at weld footprints, verified by weld-quality sampling (porosity, tensile); tin whisker risk mitigated by nickel underplate and matte tin per JEDEC guidance; any joint later converted from welded to bolted must re-trigger the plating rule — enforced in the drawing chain.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Tesla 4680 structural pack — weld-first interconnection economics where plating serves the weld process, not legacy contact specs.
